newsitem.title: USA: U.S. heart transplant said given to youngest patient.
newsitem.headline: U.S. heart transplant said given to youngest patient.

text.p: A newborn infant who received a heart transplant last weekend shortly after drawing her first breath was doing well as she recovered from the complicated operation on Thursday, her parents and doctors said.

Cheyenne Pyle was only about one hour old on Sunday when doctors at Miami's Jackson Children's Hospital began a six-hour procedure in which they opened her tiny chest, removed her defective heart and replaced it with one from another infant.
Experts on organ transplantation said they believed the operation made the little girl the youngest person ever to receive a new heart.

Cheyenne was diagnosed with a deadly heart condition, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, while she was still in her mother's womb. Her doctors put her on a waiting list for a new heart weeks before her birth was expected.

An appropriate heart became available Saturday, just 10 days after Cheyenne was put on the list, so her parents, Alberta and Stephen Pyle of Fort Lauderdale, were called to the hospital for an early Caesarean section. The girl was born at 12:32 a.m. EST (0532 GMT) on Sunday, about an hour before her transplant surgery was scheduled.

Cheyenne faced several weeks of recovery in the hospital, but doctors said being a newborn would actually help her recover. Babies' immune systems are so weak that their bodies are less likely than adults' to reject transplanted organs, doctors said.
Mrs. Pyle told a news conference that the family had high hopes the transplant would be successful and said they had never considered letting her die, even if a heart had not become available.
"That never was an option," she said.
Cheyenne's doctors said she was extremely lucky to have received a heart so quickly. Adults can spend months on transplant waiting lists, and infant hearts are even rarer.
Information about the donor of Cheyenne's heart was not made available to protect the privacy of the family, as is customary on transplant cases.
